questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to explore a different culture without going too far from home (Denmark). In the netherlands, and especially Amsterdam, they have a very different approach to rules and norms. Also, I heard that the dutch people were very friendly and open. The University of Amsterdam also had a great reputation when it comes to media science, which was appealing to me. Last but not least, I had been to Amsterdam before and found the city to be so beautiful.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Amsterdam has become my second home, and I have grown so much as a person from being here.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I found it quite easy when I understood UvA's homepage and I also got a lot of help from Online Mobility's "to do list". Of course there will always be some difficulties moving to a new country, but they were not overwhelming.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I used the ESN programme and UvA's communication science department to get to know the city and the university.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I used the Facebook page "Kamer Gezocht/Aangeboden in Amsterdam" where a lot of people posts about rooms for rent daily. Be prepared to contact a lot of people and to have a lot of meetings. If you just contact enough people you will find something, but be patient. And as always, look out for scammers.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: You might get a bit of FOMO talking with friends who live in student accommodations because they usually will have more events etc in their buildings. But I really loved living more privately. It felt way more authentic and I had the sweetest dutch roomate who helped me understand the culture a bit better. And don't worry, you will also have events and parties to go to.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I give it only 3 because it took me a long time to find something, but it ended up being a really nice place.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: This was probably the part that gave me the biggest issues and took the longest.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I had to register for courses through a website called Glass, where it was chosen randomly who would get a spot on the different courses. The website was quite new, and the staff could barely help me when I wrote them and asked questions. Also, it took me a long time to figure out which courses I was allowed to take, and there was very few courses to choose from. So it was a bit stressful when I didn't get two out of five courses and I had to find some more to apply to. In the end it all worked out though.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The UvA staff could help with most questions, but as I mentioned before, they didn't really know anything about Glass which was frustrating.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got 3/5 of the ones I wished for, and ended up with 2 I didn't really care about.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Begin to look into the courses as early as possible, and dont panic if you can't figure out Glass immediately.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The courses didn't really seem to hard. But then at the exam, the level was so high with really difficult questions. Normally my grades are pretty good, but here I barely passed some of my courses. I guess it is nice to be challenged, but it was a bit stressful at times.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: There were way more people at each course which made it a bit less personal. In some courses I had really great teachers, and in some I had really bad ones. It varied a lot. It was also more important to read the curriculum at UvA to understand the lectures and to pass the course. Also, we had more small assignments at UvA than UCPH.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: "Education and Work" (Sociology), "Topic What does it mean to be literate? Social and policy consequences of 21st century literacies", "Topic Content Marketing", "Topic Algorithmic Persuasion in the Digital Society" & "Topic Health Communication: From Theory to Practice".

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend "Topic Algorithmic Persuasion in the Digital Society" because the teachers were great and it was super interesting to learn about algorithms and their imprint on society.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I did a lot of trips outside of Amsterdam, and the train tickets were quite expensive.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Beer is cheaper than in Denmark. The food in the supermarket costs about the same. If you rent a Swapfiets for about 190 kr a month, you will save a lot of money on transportation.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I followed the ESN introduction week which really helped me to meet new friends. They had lots of events (mostly parties) some were organised too well, but it was still fun. I went on this party boat on Kings day with ESN, and the boat was really not as nice as they had said.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Do the ESN introduction week. I basically met all my friends there. If you are on exchange in the spring, go and celebrate Kings day! And go out for coffee and beers as much as you can, go for long walks in the outer skirts of Amsterdam and enjoy their parks!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go to Utrecht, Leiden, Rotterdam and the coast. They have a lot of nice cities that are fun to visit for one day. Also, in tulip season, go to Keukenhof! I will also recommend Anne Franks house, Van Gogh museum and NXT museum.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy. It is a lot like Denmark. It is more scary to bike in Amsterdam though, as people don't seem to follow rules as much.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: The only time I really got to talk with local students was during class. So maybe try that.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The biking and the fact that the dutch people are very straight forwards and tells you exaclty what they think. In the beginning I could be a bit offended by my roomate when he made fun of danish food or language, but in the end I was about to just laugh about it.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The open minded people. You could always find someone to talk to at a bar or club. (And bitterballen).

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Be open minded to people who might not look like your typical friends. Be prepared to read a lot (do it in a nice cafe!). Be a part of ESN, even though it sometimes feels a bit forced.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: To meet new people from all over the world, who had a different way of viewing the world. It really put things into perspective, and you learn so much about yourself through this.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: To be away from family, friends and boyfriend and to follow what the people back home are doing on social media.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Enjoy your stay :-)

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
